VI.2.2 Model-independent bounds on the helium fraction

Instead of deriving the primordial helium abundance from BBN codes using constraints on (Ωb​h2,Neff)(\Omega_{b}h^{2},N_{\rm eff}), we can measure it directly with the CMB. Variations in YHeY_{\rm He} alter the density of free electrons between helium and hydrogen recombination, thereby affecting the damping tail of the CMB anisotropies. By sampling the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}+YHeY_{\rm He} model and converting the helium mass fraction into the helium nucleon fraction, we find

Yp=0.2312±0.0092(68%,P-ACT-LB),Y_{p}=0.2312\pm 0.0092\quad(68\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LB}), (45)

in good agreement with the astrophysical helium abundance measurements. Since both the helium abundance and the number of relativistic degrees of freedom influence the CMB damping tail, allowing both to vary simultaneously leads to weaker constraints

Yp=0.227±0.014Neff=3.14±0.25} (68%, P-ACT-LB).\left.\begin{aligned} Y_{p}&=0.227\pm 0.014\\ N_{\rm eff}&=3.14\pm 0.25\end{aligned}\quad\right\}\mbox{{\; (68\%, {P-ACT-LB}).}} (46)

This is still consistent with direct helium abundance measurements and with the expected number of neutrinos, but with larger errors. The relatively low values of YpY_{p} in this case have the same origin as the low value of NeffN_{\rm eff} in the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}+NeffN_{\rm eff} model, since lower values of both of these parameters reduce the damping, which is preferred by the ACT data. The joint constraints in the Neff−YHe{N_{\rm eff}-Y_{\rm He}} plane are shown in Fig. 30, where the anti-correlation between these two parameters is clearly evident.

Considering the PDG collection of helium abundance measurements as an external dataset, it is possible to sample the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}+NeffN_{\rm eff}+YHeY_{\rm He} model imposing a prior on YpY_{p}, which leads to

Yp=0.2444±0.0029Neff=2.86±0.14} (68%, P-ACT-LB-He),\left.\begin{aligned} Y_{p}&=0.2444\pm 0.0029\\ N_{\rm eff}&=2.86\pm 0.14\end{aligned}\quad\right\}\mbox{{\; (68\%, {P-ACT-LB-He}),}} (47)

where the degeneracy between NeffN_{\rm eff} and YHeY_{\rm He} is efficiently broken by helium measurements (see Fig. 30) and the retrieved NeffN_{\rm eff} constraint is consistent with the one obtained in the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}+NeffN_{\rm eff} model.

VI.3 Axion-like particles

We constrain contributions to the total dark-sector content from ultralight axion-like particles (with masses between 10−28<max/eV<10−24{10^{-28}~<m_{\mathrm{ax}}~/{\rm eV}<10^{-24}}). This ultralight pseudo-scalar dark matter model is well-motivated by high-energy physics, as axions can generically arise from a variety of broken symmetries or compactified extra dimensions, the so-called “axiverse” [30, 142]. These ultralight axions suppress structure formation below their de Broglie wavelength, which manifests on astrophysical scales. The axion Jeans scale λJ\lambda_{J}, below which structure is smoothed out, depends on the axion mass: λJ∝max−1/2\lambda_{J}\propto m_{\mathrm{ax}}^{-1/2} [24, 142, 30, 336, 208, 297, 215, 256, 327]. The dynamics of the axion are described through the Klein-Gordon equation

ϕ′′+2​ℋ​ϕ′+a2​d​Vd​ϕ=0.{\phi}^{\prime\prime}+2\mathcal{H}{\phi}^{\prime}+a^{2}\frac{dV}{d\phi}=0. (48)

Here ϕ\phi is the axion field, with ϕ0\phi_{0} indicating its homogeneous component, and primes denote derivatives with respect to conformal time. In the simplest case with a quadratic axion potential, this simplifies to

ϕ′′+2​ℋ​ϕ′+a2​max2​ϕ=0,{\phi}^{\prime\prime}+2\mathcal{H}{\phi}^{\prime}+a^{2}m_{\rm ax}^{2}\phi=0, (49)

where ℋ≡a′/a=a​H\mathcal{H}\equiv{a}^{\prime}/a=aH is the conformal Hubble parameter, which acts as a friction term in the oscillator equation governing the axion dynamics. When the Hubble term drops (as the universe cools) to near the axion mass max≃3​H​(aosc)m_{\rm ax}\simeq 3H(a_{\rm osc}), the axion field begins to coherently oscillate, and begins to behave as a dark matter component (with ρax∝a−3\rho_{\rm ax}\propto a^{-3}), whereas it behaves as a frozen-in “dark-energy-like” component at earlier times. This links the axion mass directly to its observational impact on the CMB and large-scale structure clustering. We solve for the relic axion density by solving the field equations given that

Ωax=[12​(ϕ0′a)2+max22​ϕ02]max=3​H​aosc3ρcrit,\Omega_{\rm ax}=\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\phi_{0}^{\prime}}{a}\right)^{2}+\frac{m_{\rm ax}^{2}}{2}\phi_{0}^{2}\right]_{m_{\rm ax}=3H}\frac{a_{\rm osc}^{3}}{\rho_{\mathrm{crit}}}\,, (50)

where ρcrit\rho_{\mathrm{crit}} is the critical density at z=0z=0. We model the effects of axions via the axionCAMB Boltzmann solver,3030 30 https://github.com/dgrin1/axionCAMB which has been used in several previous analyses of the impacts of axions on the CMB and LSS [208, 206, 378, 256, e.g.,]. There have been several improvements in the full Boltzmann solution [284, e.g.,] that are particularly relevant in extreme ranges of parameter space that we do not consider here. We leave a full comparison between codes for future work.

In order to correctly model the power on small scales [207, 128, and to not introduce spurious signals of axion physics, see], we use a modified halo model including mixed dark matter [443]. The computational cost of both the halo model code and axionCAMB requires using an emulator for efficient computation. We employ the axionEmu emulator,3131 31 https://github.com/keirkwame/axionEmu which is based on a modified version of CosmoPower.

We present our constraints on the allowed fraction of the dark matter density that is comprised of axions in Fig. 31. For the lightest axion species max≲10−28​eV{m_{\rm ax}\lesssim 10^{-28}~\mathrm{eV}} (not studied here, but see, e.g., 208) this represents a limit on how axions can constitute the dark energy. For the max≳10−27​eV{m_{\rm ax}\gtrsim 10^{-27}~\mathrm{eV}} axions that we consider here, constraints on the axion fraction reflect a disentangling of axion effects from standard cold dark matter in large-scale clustering.

Using the primary CMB spectra from Planck alone or P-ACT, we find

max=10−26​eV:\displaystyle m_{\rm ax}=10^{-26}\,\,\textrm{eV}:
Ωax/(Ωax+Ωc)\displaystyle\Omega_{\mathrm{ax}}/(\Omega_{\mathrm{ax}}+\Omega_{c}) <\displaystyle< 0.070(95%,Planck)\displaystyle 0.070\quad(95\%,\,\textsf{Planck}) (51)
<\displaystyle< 0.052(95%,P-ACT).\displaystyle 0.052\quad(95\%,\,\textsf{P-ACT}).

The upper limits for max=10−27​eVm_{\rm ax}=10^{-27}\,\,\mathrm{eV} are comparable between Planck and P-ACT at 4.5%4.5\%, while P-ACT reduces the allowed fraction of axion-like dark matter to roughly 5% (95% CL) for the mass max=10−26​eVm_{\rm ax}=10^{-26}\,\mathrm{eV}. For masses lighter than max<10−26,m_{\rm ax}<10^{-26}, the axion starts to roll in its potential at later times, leading to changes in the primary CMB spectra on scales where Planck is most constraining. Some of the improvement in the constraints comes from the degeneracy between the axion density and the scalar spectral index. As the preferred value of nsn_{s} slightly increases between Planck and P-ACT, the limits on the axion density also tighten. The impact of increased sensitivity in the temperature and polarization power spectra is more pronounced for the CMB lensing deflection power spectrum, particularly for max≥10−25​eVm_{\rm ax}\geq 10^{-25}\,\mathrm{eV}. A full presentation of axion constraints including the ACT DR6 lensing power spectrum, and detailed modeling of the nonlinear clustering that impacts the lensing deflection on small scales, will be provided in a future paper [258].

VI.4 Dark matter

Many compelling dark matter (DM) models can be tested with cosmological probes, including scenarios where DM interacts with baryons or annihilates into photons as described in this section, and scenarios where DM interacts with dark radiation (§VI.5) or with dark energy (§VII.3).

VI.4.1 DM-baryon interactions

Dark matter models beyond the standard paradigm of cold, collisionless DM (CDM) include scenarios in which DM interacts with baryons [116, 51, 181, 12]. As done in previous ACT analyses [274], we consider the specific case in which DM elastically scatters with protons [180, 73] through a contact interaction. These models were previously explored using both linear cosmology [75, 404, 146, 180, 73, 74, 324, 377, 274, 409, 88, 210, 56] and near-field cosmology [293, 321, 319, 181]. In a DM-baryon scattering scenario, the two corresponding cosmological fluids exchange heat and momentum, leading to collisional damping of small-scale perturbations in the early universe. The strength of the interaction is quantified with the momentum-transfer cross-section σMT=σ0​(v/c)n\sigma_{\mathrm{MT}}=\sigma_{0}(v/c)^{n}, where vv is the relative particle velocity (sourced primarily by thermal velocities at the redshifts of interest), nn is the power-law index determined by the interaction theory, and the cross-section normalization σ0\sigma_{0} is a free parameter of the model.

We consider models with n=−4{n=-4}, 0, and 2 and fix the DM particle mass to mχ=1m_{\chi}=1 MeV. We choose a sub-proton mass because direct detection experiments probe values of mχm_{\chi} greater than 1 GeV, and constraints from NeffN_{\rm eff} exclude thermal-relic DM with masses lower than ∼1\sim 1 MeV [267, 26]. The choice of mχ=1m_{\chi}=1 MeV allows us to explore the extreme end of what direct detection does not reach. We then choose to explore the set of nn values that correspond to the most salient DM-baryon scattering models: millicharged DM (n=−4{n=-4}), a velocity-independent and spin-independent contact interaction (n=0{n=0}), and DM with a velocity-dependent contact interaction (n=2{n=2}) [146]. We use a modified version of class [180, 74] that incorporates the effect of DM-baryon scattering in the linear-theory Einstein-Boltzmann equations. We assume a broad, flat, positive prior on σ0\sigma_{0} for each value of nn. Each interaction model is thus a single-parameter extension of Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}, for a given nn and DM particle mass.

We present constraints corresponding to the three interaction scenarios in Fig. 32. For n=−4{n=-4}, we find that ACT data do not improve on Planck constraints, giving σ0​(n=−4)<6.1×10−42​cm2​(95%,P-ACT)\sigma_{0}({n=-4})<6.1\times 10^{-42}~\rm{cm}^{2}~(95\%,\textsf{P-ACT}); similarly, the addition of CMB lensing and BAO data has a negligible impact on the constraint. This is because the n=−4{n=-4} model produces a scale-independent suppression at high ℓ\ell, and the high-multipole measurements from ACT do not add significantly to the signal-to-noise for this scenario. On the other hand, the n=0n=0 model produces a strong ℓ\ell-dependent power suppression in both temperature and polarization [196, e.g.,], and thus ACT alone has comparable constraining power to Planck, leading to an upper bound of σ0​(n=0)<1.7×10−26​cm2​(95%,ACT)\sigma_{0}({n=0})<1.7\times 10^{-26}~\rm{cm}^{2}~(95\%,\textsf{ACT}). A combined analysis of ACT and Planck data leads to a factor of two improvement in the upper bounds,

σ0​(n=0)\displaystyle\sigma_{0}(n=0) <\displaystyle< 9.9×10−27​cm2​(95%,P-ACT),\displaystyle 9.9\times 10^{-27}\,\,\rm{cm}^{2}\ (95\%,\textsf{P-ACT}), (52)
<\displaystyle< 8.5×10−27​cm2​(95%,P-ACT-LB).\displaystyle 8.5\times 10^{-27}\,\,\rm{cm}^{2}\ (95\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LB}).

For n=2{n=2}, ACT only marginally improves on Planck constraints, giving σ0​(n=2)<1.5×10−21​cm2\sigma_{0}({n=2})<1.5\times 10^{-21}~\rm{cm}^{2} (95%, P-ACT). The addition of CMB lensing and BAO data again has a minimal impact, giving σ0​(n=2)<1.2×10−21​cm2​(95%,P-ACT-LB)\sigma_{0}({n=2})<1.2\times 10^{-21}~\rm{cm}^{2}~(95\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LB}). As ACT data are particularly sensitive to power suppression on small scales, the difference in constraining power for n=0n=0 and n=2n=2 stems from the baryon-loading-like effect occurring in the n=2{n=2} model, which leads to an enhancement of power at intermediate multipoles, rather than a strong suppression seen in the n=0n=0 case [74].

The limits presented here are the tightest bounds on DM-baryon interactions obtained to date from linear cosmology. In particular, these bounds are consistent with and comparable to the results of joint analyses of Planck, BOSS, and DES data [197, 196]. Meanwhile, the bounds obtained from highly nonlinear systems, such as the Milky Way satellite galaxy population, are stronger for all models that produce strong scale-dependent suppression (in this case, n=0,2n=0,2), as they lead to a notable decrement of small halos in the late universe [293, 321, 320]. However, the non-linear modeling required for satellite analyses does not yet allow the exploration of the full cosmological parameter space, and the bounds obtained from near-field cosmology are thus not an apples-to-apples comparison to the present results. Moreover, mixed DM with a subcomponent interacting through velocity-independent (n=0n=0) scattering was also found to yield a lower value of S8S_{8}, by suppressing the linear matter power spectrum on semi-nonlinear scales [197, 196]. The ACT DR6 analysis results presented here are consistent with the preferred parameter space of interacting DM that reduces S8S_{8} by a non-negligible amount, for the case where all DM interacts with protons. However, models that are most interesting in this context feature mixed DM and dedicated analyses of these scenarios are left for future work.

VI.4.2 DM annihilation

If DM annihilates into Standard Model particles, energy released by the annihilation process is injected into the photon-baryon plasma around the time of recombination. This energy injection affects the CMB by altering the ionization history so as to broaden the width of the last-scattering surface and introducing a unique signature in matter clustering. The main observational signatures in the CMB power spectra are: (i) damping of high-ℓ\ell power in both temperature and polarization; (ii) enhancement of the polarization power spectrum at ℓ≲400\ell\lesssim 400; (iii) shifts of the low-ℓ\ell acoustic peaks in polarization (e.g., 331, 295, 183). The high-ℓ\ell signature is degenerate with other parameters that alter the damping tail, such as nsn_{s}; thus, most of the constraining power beyond Planck for this model is anticipated to come from large-scale polarization measurements. Because of this, we do not expect major improvements in the constraints for this model from ACT DR6, given the scales probed by our data.

We follow earlier literature [161, 295] and constrain the annihilation parameter

pann=feff​⟨σ​v⟩mχp_{\mathrm{ann}}=f_{\mathrm{eff}}\frac{\langle\sigma v\rangle}{m_{\chi}} (53)

where mχm_{\chi} is the DM particle mass, ⟨σ​v⟩\langle\sigma v\rangle is the thermally-averaged annihilation cross-section, and fefff_{\mathrm{eff}} is the fraction of the energy due to annihilation that is injected into the plasma [354]. The transferred energy fraction f⁡(z)f(z) is indeed redshift-dependent, but this redshift dependence only weakly impacts the CMB and can thus be approximated by a constant fraction f⁡(z)≈fefff(z)\approx f_{\mathrm{eff}} [407, 408]. Thus, fefff_{\mathrm{eff}} corresponds to the energy transferred to the plasma around the redshifts at which the CMB is most sensitive to DM annihilation (z≈500−600z\approx 500-600) [161]. We assume that this energy from DM annihilation is transferred to the plasma immediately, known as the “on-the-spot approximation” [354]. We set a broad, flat prior on pann∈[0,10−26​cm3/s/GeV]p_{\rm ann}\in[0,10^{-26}~{\rm cm^{3}/s/GeV}] and use the implementation of this model in the current standard version of class.

The results of this analysis are summarized in Fig. 33. We find no evidence of DM annihilation from the new ACT DR6 spectra, with pann<1.4×10−27​cm3/s/GeV⁡(95%,ACT)p_{\rm{ann}}<1.4\times 10^{-27}\ \rm{cm^{3}/s/GeV}\ (95\%,\textsf{ACT}). When combining with Planck, we find that the joint upper limit does not improve upon the Planck-only constraint of pann<3.9×10−28​cm3/s/GeV⁡(95%)p_{\rm{ann}}<3.9\times 10^{-28}\ \rm{cm^{3}/s/GeV}\ (95\%),3232 32 We find a slightly weaker bound for Planck alone than that in Eq. (89a) of [354]; this may be due to a slight shift of the central value arising from our use of Sroll2 for the low-ℓ\ell EE data, which is particularly important in constraining this model. but this is primarily due to the peak of the posterior for pannp_{\rm ann} shifting slightly away from zero, as can be seen in Fig. 33. The joint constraint gives pann<4.1×10−28​cm3/s/GeV⁡(95%,P-ACT)p_{\rm{ann}}<4.1\times 10^{-28}\ \rm{cm^{3}/s/GeV}\ (95\%,\textsf{P-ACT}). The addition of CMB lensing and BAO data helps to tighten the constraints and pushes the peak of the posterior back to zero, yielding pann<3.6×10−28​cm3/s/GeV⁡(95%,P-ACT-LB)p_{\rm{ann}}<3.6\times 10^{-28}\ \rm{cm^{3}/s/GeV}\ (95\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LB}). Further addition of SNIa data does not tighten this limit. While the ACT DR6 data do not significantly improve constraints on pannp_{\rm ann} beyond those from Planck, future improvements from large-scale CMB polarization data are expected (see, e.g., 295, 183).

VI.5 Interacting dark radiation

VI.5.1 Self-interacting DR

A wide range of dark radiation (DR) models have been constructed, beyond the simple free-streaming case parameterized by NeffN_{\rm eff} [231, 89, 118, 263, 21, 234, 87, 383, 393, 454, e.g.,]. These models generically involve self-interactions amongst the DR, interactions between the DR and (a subset of) the DM, or combinations thereof, potentially with non-trivial time-dependence (e.g., due to the temperature of the DR-DM sector falling below the mass of a massive mediator particle). As a first step toward investigating these scenarios, we consider a simple model of (strongly) self-interacting DR (SIDR), for example due to a new gauge interaction in the dark sector. At the background level, this model is identical to NeffN_{\rm eff}, with a free parameter Nidr≥0N_{\rm idr}\geq 0 describing the number of additional relativistic species (and hence the additional DR energy density). However, the SIDR and free-streaming DR models differ at the perturbative level: the SIDR forms a perfect relativistic fluid with w=1/3=cs2{w=1/3=c_{s}^{2}}, with interactions sufficiently strong that no anisotropic stress (or higher-order Boltzmann moments) can be supported. Thus, the perturbative dynamics are characterized fully by the continuity and Euler equations. Unlike free-streaming DR, SIDR can cluster on small scales, thus reducing the impact of Silk damping on the high-ℓ\ell power spectra (at fixed DR energy density). In addition, SIDR generates a smaller phase shift in the power spectra. Thus, CMB fits to the SIDR model can accommodate larger amounts of DR than the free-streaming DR model, which can thus allow higher values of H0H_{0} [21, 392, 19, e.g.,].

We consider a simple SIDR model parameterized solely by NidrN_{\rm idr}, with Nidr≥0N_{\rm idr}\geq 0. We assume no interactions between the SIDR and the DM. We use the implementation of this model in class3333 33 We set idm_dr_tight_coupling_trigger_tau_c_over_tau_h = 0.005 and idm_dr_tight_coupling_trigger_tau_c_over_tau_k = 0.008 to ensure high accuracy, identical to the values we use for the analogous class accuracy parameters in the SM sector (see Appendix A). and we adopt a flat, uninformative prior Nidr∈[0,6]N_{\rm idr}\in[0,6]. We assume that the SM neutrino sector consists of one massive state carrying 0.06 eV and two massless states, with Neff=3.044N_{\rm eff}=3.044.

Constraints on this model are presented in Fig. 34. From the ACT DR6 primary CMB power spectra alone, we find

Nidr\displaystyle N_{\rm idr} <\displaystyle< 0.339(95%,ACT)\displaystyle 0.339\quad\quad\quad\ (95\%,\,\textsf{ACT})
H0\displaystyle H_{0} =\displaystyle= 66.85−1.0+0.85(68%,ACT).\displaystyle 66.85^{+0.85}_{-1.0}\,\,\quad(68\%,\,\textsf{ACT}). (54)

Including Planck primary CMB power spectra, we obtain

Nidr\displaystyle N_{\rm idr} <\displaystyle< 0.114(95%,P-ACT)\displaystyle 0.114\quad\quad\quad\ (95\%,\,\textsf{P-ACT})
H0\displaystyle H_{0} =\displaystyle= 68.00−0.63+0.55(68%,P-ACT).\displaystyle 68.00^{+0.55}_{-0.63}\,\quad(68\%,\,\textsf{P-ACT}). (55)

The joint P-ACT constraint represents more than a factor-of-three improvement over the constraint from Planck alone, for which we find Nidr<0.379N_{\rm idr}<0.379 at 95% confidence. The origin of this tight constraint is the lack of preference for excess high-ℓ\ell damping in the DR6 power spectra; since SIDR can only increase damping (due to the physical bound Nidr>0N_{\rm idr}>0), its existence is thus disfavored by the data. From the primary CMB, we thus see no evidence of additional SIDR species, extending our results for the free-streaming DR case (NeffN_{\rm eff}) to a very different physical regime.

Including additional low-redshift datasets does not significantly tighten the bound on NidrN_{\rm idr}, but further tightens the error bar on H0H_{0} and other cosmological parameters. From the combination of ACT and Planck CMB spectra, ACT and Planck CMB lensing, and DESI BAO, we obtain

Nidr\displaystyle N_{\rm idr} <\displaystyle< 0.134(95%,P-ACT-LB)\displaystyle 0.134\quad\quad\ \ (95\%,\,\textsf{P-ACT-LB})
H0\displaystyle H_{0} =\displaystyle= 68.59−0.50+0.41​(68%,P-ACT-LB).\displaystyle 68.59^{+0.41}_{-0.50}\,\ (68\%,\,\textsf{P-ACT-LB}). (56)

The upper limit on NidrN_{\rm idr} weakens slightly compared to that found for P-ACT above, due to small shifts in the best-fit parameter values. Further including SNIa data in the analysis yields negligible changes to these constraints.

The MAP SIDR model found for P-ACT, as well as that found for P-ACT-LB, yields negligible improvement in the quality of fit over Λ\LambdaCDM — in fact, we find that the MAP SIDR model lies at the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} limit of the parameter space in both cases, i.e., with Nidr=0N_{\rm idr}=0, indicating no preference for this model extension. We emphasize again that this lack of preference arises from the lack of excess damping seen at high-ℓ\ell in ACT: because SIDR can only increase damping over that in Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}, the model cannot accommodate decreased damping (unlike NeffN_{\rm eff}, which can do so via a value of Neff<3.044N_{\rm eff}<3.044).

These are the tightest bounds on SIDR presented to date. The ability of this model to increase the value of H0H_{0} inferred from cosmological data is strongly limited by these observations, with the new ACT DR6 spectra playing a crucial role in significantly tightening the constraints compared to those from Planck.

VI.5.2 Interacting DR-DM

A wide range of dark sector models have been considered in the literature, featuring various types of interactions between dark radiation and dark matter species [118, 89, 263, e.g.,]. As a first step in probing this space of models, here we consider the fiducial scenario studied in Rubira et al. [383], in which an SIDR fluid (identical to that studied above) interacts with all of the DM via an interaction with a momentum transfer rate Γ⁡(a)=Γ0,nadm​a−2\Gamma(a)=\Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm}a^{-2} between the DM and the DR [90]. Microphysically, such an interaction can be realized in dark-sector models featuring non-Abelian gauge bosons (hence the “nadm” subscript) that mediate interactions between Dirac fermion DM particles [89, 263]. In this particular model, Γ\Gamma has a redshift (or temperature) dependence that matches that of the Hubble rate during radiation domination — see [89] for an explicit calculation of the momentum transfer rate in the “nadm” model. As a consequence, the interaction between the DR and the DM is relevant while modes covering a broad range of scales enter the horizon (essentially during all of radiation domination), which leads to a roughly scale-invariant suppression of power for such modes. This makes the model a promising candidate to decrease the CMB-inferred value of S8S_{8} [89, 383]. The SIDR abundance (set by NidrN_{\rm idr}) determines the scale where power is suppressed, while the interaction strength Γ0,nadm\Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm} determines the amount of suppression [89].3434 34 Note that the IDR-IDM interaction studied here is not relevant in the late universe, and thus late-time growth is not affected; modifications to structure formation are captured by the change in the linear matter power spectrum.

We use the implementation of this interacting DR – interacting DM (IDR-IDM) model in class [263, 29]. The model contains two additional free parameters beyond those of base Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}: NidrN_{\rm idr} (as in the SIDR model above) and Γ0,nadm\Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm}. We adopt the same priors and model assumptions as for the SIDR scenario for all common parameters, while for Γ0,nadm\Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm}, we adopt an uninformative, uniform prior Γ0,nadm/(Mpc−1)∈[0.0,5.0×10−7]\Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm}/({\rm Mpc}^{-1})\in\left[0.0,5.0\times 10^{-7}\right].

We find no preference for the IDR-IDM scenario in the ACT DR6 spectra. Constraints on this model are shown in Fig. 35. Joint analysis of ACT and Planck yields

Nidr<0.0977Γ0,nadm<4.45×10−7​Mpc−1} (95%, P-ACT).\left.\begin{aligned} N_{\rm idr}&<0.0977\\ \Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm}&<4.45\times 10^{-7}~{\rm Mpc}^{-1}\end{aligned}\quad\right\}\mbox{{\; (95\%, {P-ACT}).}} (57)

This is a significant improvement over analogous results from Planck alone, for which we find Nidr<0.367N_{\rm idr}<0.367 at 95% CL and no bound on Γ0,nadm\Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm} (at 95% CL). We find negligible reduction in S8S_{8} in the P-ACT fit to the IDR-IDM model, with S8=0.814−0.015+0.023S_{8}=0.814^{+0.023}_{-0.015} at 68% CL. Inclusion of CMB lensing and DESI BAO data in the combined dataset yields:

Nidr<0.135Γ0,nadm<4.09×10−7​Mpc−1} (95%, P-ACT-LB).\left.\begin{aligned} N_{\rm idr}&<0.135\\ \Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm}&<4.09\times 10^{-7}~{\rm Mpc}^{-1}\end{aligned}\quad\right\}\mbox{{\; (95\%, {P-ACT-LB}).}} (58)

The bound on S8S_{8} tightens considerably compared to P-ACT, with S8=0.808−0.0095+0.013S_{8}=0.808^{+0.013}_{-0.0095} at 68% CL, further limiting this model’s ability to yield low values of this parameter.

We note that Bayesian constraints on the IDR-IDM model can suffer from volume effects, since Γ0,nadm\Gamma_{\rm 0,nadm} becomes degenerate in the Nidr→0N_{\rm idr}\rightarrow 0 limit. We thus confirm that the best-fit IDR-IDM model to P-ACT or P-ACT-LB does not yield a significantly better fit to these data than Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}. In fact, as found for SIDR, we find that the MAP model in the IDR-IDM scenario for both P-ACT and P-ACT-LB is indistinguishable from Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} within our numerical precision. Overall, we see no evidence of extended dark-sector physics in this analysis.

VII Gravity and late-time physics

VII.1 Geometry: spatial curvature

In the inflationary scenario, at the end of inflation the universe is predicted to emerge in a state very close to spatially flat [277, 17]. This hypothesis is tested empirically by allowing the curvature density parameter, Ωk\Omega_{k}, which is fixed to zero in the baseline Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} model, to be a free parameter. As discussed in L25, the new ACT DR6 power spectra alone prefer a flat geometry, breaking degeneracies via lensing effects in the power spectra; in a joint fit with Planck, ACT DR6 moves the Planck contours toward vanishing curvature. When adding BAO and CMB lensing data to the primary CMB, the degeneracy with the matter density is more effectively broken, as shown in Fig. 36, and the constraints tighten significantly, yielding

Ωk=0.0019±0.0015(68%,P-ACT-LB),\Omega_{k}=0.0019\pm 0.0015\quad(68\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LB}), (59)

similar to Ωk=0.0022±0.0015\Omega_{k}=0.0022\pm 0.0015 (68%, Planck-LB). These limits derived from the combination of CMB and low-redshift data tightly constrain the universe’s spatial geometry, and are fully consistent with spatial flatness.

This result can be converted into a new limit on the present-day radius of spatial curvature of the universe, OPENRk=c/H0/(​|Ωtot−1|)R_{k}=c/H_{0}/\sqrt{(}|\Omega_{\rm tot}-1|) where Ωtot\Omega_{\rm tot} is the total cosmic energy density, such that Ωk=1−Ωtot\Omega_{k}=1-\Omega_{\rm tot}. With P-ACT-LB we find at 95% confidence Rk>105R_{k}>105 Gpc or equivalently Rk>343R_{k}>343 billion light-years for a closed universe (Ωtot>1\Omega_{\rm tot}>1 or Ωk<0\Omega_{k}<0) and Rk>66R_{k}>66 Gpc or Rk>215R_{k}>215 billion light-years for an open universe (Ωtot<1\Omega_{\rm tot}<1 or Ωk>0\Omega_{k}>0).

VII.2 Late-time dark energy

Within the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} model, the dark energy density is constant over time, described by a cosmological constant Λ\Lambda with an equation of state w≡−1w\equiv-1 at all times. A common way of exploring the dark energy component is to relax the assumption on its equation of state, considering a time evolution of the pressure-density ratio P/ρ=w⁡(a)P/\rho=w(a) with [102, 281]3535 35 See, e.g., [402] for consideration of time-evolving dark energy beyond the (w0,wa)(w_{0},w_{a}) parametrization.

w⁡(a)=w0+wa​(1−a).w(a)=w_{0}+w_{a}(1-a). (60)

This is equivalent to a cosmological constant Λ\Lambda when setting today’s value of the equation of state to w0=−1{w_{0}=-1} and its time dependence to wa=0{w_{a}=0}. This expansion can then be used for explorations varying either only w0w_{0} or both w0w_{0} and waw_{a}, as we do below. Opening these degrees of freedom in the dark energy component causes strong degeneracies between parameters when using only CMB data and therefore we mostly report results for combinations with CMB lensing and external probes of the expansion history, including both BAO and SNIa. In particular, as shown in [137] in fits to models with additional degrees of freedom in the dark energy equation of state, SNIa are essential to break degeneracies with H0H_{0} and the matter density. We do not expect significant improvements from the new ACT power spectra for late-time dark energy, but we report constraints here given interest in this model following the DESI Year-1 results.

When w≡w0w\equiv w_{0} is free to vary as a single-parameter extension to Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} (without time dependence — wa=0{w_{a}=0} — and imposing a flat prior w0∈[−3,1]w_{0}{\in[-3,1]})3636 36 To get theory predictions for this model we use camb with the Parametrized Post-Friedmann approach [158] to compute dark energy perturbations (dark_energy_model=DarkEnergyPPF)., we obtain the contours shown in Fig. 1 for P-ACT-LB. Adding also SNIa data, we find

w0=−0.986±0.025​(68%,P-ACT-LBS),w_{0}=-0.986\pm 0.025\;(68\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LBS}), (61)

in good agreement with the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} expectation, and with the same error bar as previous measurements using CMB from Planck (w0=−0.997±0.025w_{0}=-0.997\pm 0.025, 137).

When we expand the model further, with both w0w_{0} and waw_{a} varying (with a flat prior wa∈[−3,2]w_{a}\in[-3,2]), we find

w0=−0.837±0.061wa=−0.66−0.24+0.27} (68%, P-ACT-LBS),\left.\begin{aligned} w_{0}&=-0.837\pm 0.061\\ w_{a}&=-0.66^{+0.27}_{-0.24}\end{aligned}\quad\right\}\mbox{{\; (68\%, {P-ACT-LBS}),}} (62)

with marginalized posteriors shown in Fig. 37. We see a moderate preference for the w0​wa​CDMw_{0}w_{a}\mathrm{CDM} model over Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}, similar to what was reported in [137] using CMB data from Planck (w0=−0.827±0.063w_{0}=-0.827\pm 0.063, wa=−0.75−0.25+0.29w_{a}=-0.75^{+0.29}_{-0.25}).3737 37 Quantitatively, comparing the MAP w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM and Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} models, we find Δ​χ2=−7.0\Delta\chi^{2}=-7.0 (2.2​σ2.2\sigma) for P-ACT-LBS, while [137] find Δ​χ2=−8.7\Delta\chi^{2}=-8.7 (2.5​σ2.5\sigma) for Planck-LBS. This result is driven partially by the DESI data and partially by the SNIa data. Substituting the BAO dataset with BOSS BAO, the posteriors are consistent with the cosmological constant scenario. The specific CMB dataset used for this analysis has essentially no impact: Planck alone, P-ACT, or W-ACT yield similar results.

With the combined P-ACT-LBS dataset, we find a well-constrained value of H0=67.73±0.68H_{0}=67.73\pm 0.68 km/s/Mpc and H0=68.02±0.72H_{0}=68.02\pm 0.72 km/s/Mpc for the w0w_{0} and w0−wa{w_{0}-w_{a}} extensions, respectively. Similarly to [137], we also find that SNIa reduce by a factor of ∼2\sim 2 the uncertainty on H0H_{0} and shift the mean to lower values by ∼3\sim 3 km/s/Mpc (see Fig. 1).

VII.3 Interacting DE-DM

An extension of Λ\LambdaCDM with kinetic interactions between the DM and DE fluids was initially considered in [406]. This model introduces a coupling constant, ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}, describing pure momentum transfer between the DM and DE. This coupling leaves the homogeneous background cosmological evolution unchanged, but alters the dark sector perturbation evolution equations as follows [406]:

δDM′\displaystyle\delta_{\mathrm{DM}}^{\prime} =−θDM+3​ϕ′,\displaystyle=-\theta_{\mathrm{DM}}+3\phi^{\prime}, (63)
δDE′\displaystyle\delta_{\rm DE}^{\prime} =−[(1+w)+9​ℋ2k2​(1−w2)]​θDE\displaystyle=-\left[(1+w)+9\frac{\mathcal{H}^{2}}{k^{2}}\left(1-w^{2}\right)\right]\theta_{\rm DE}
+3​(1+w)​ϕ′−3​ℋ​(1−w)​δDE,\displaystyle\;\;\;\;+3(1+w)\phi^{\prime}-3\mathcal{H}(1-w)\delta_{\rm DE}, (64)
θDM′\displaystyle\theta_{\mathrm{DM}}^{\prime} =−ℋ​θDM+k2​ϕ+a​ΓDMDEρ¯DM​Δ​θ,\displaystyle=-\mathcal{H}\theta_{\mathrm{DM}}+k^{2}\phi+\frac{a\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}}{\bar{\rho}_{\rm DM}}\Delta\theta, (65)
θDE′=\displaystyle\theta_{\mathrm{DE}}^{\prime}= 2​ℋ​θDE+k2(1+w)​δDE+k2​ϕ−a​ΓDMDE(1+w)​ρ¯DE​Δ​θ,\displaystyle 2\mathcal{H}\theta_{\mathrm{DE}}+\frac{k^{2}}{\left(1+w\right)}\delta_{\mathrm{DE}}+k^{2}\phi-\frac{a\Gamma_{\mathrm{DMDE}}}{(1+w)\bar{\rho}_{\rm DE}}\Delta\theta, (66)

where ww is the DE equation of state, δ≡ρ/ρ¯−1\delta\equiv\rho/\bar{\rho}-1 is the energy density contrast, θ≡∇⋅𝐯\theta\equiv\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v} is the velocity divergence, Δ​θ≡θDE−θDM\Delta\theta\equiv\theta_{\rm DE}-\theta_{\rm DM}, ℋ\mathcal{H} is the conformal Hubble factor (ℋ=a​H\mathcal{H}=aH), ϕ\phi is the Newtonian gravitational potential, and ′ denotes differentiation with respect to conformal time.

This type of interaction leads to slower structure growth, and this idea was revisited in [59, 361, 58] as a potential way to reduce the value of S8S_{8} inferred from CMB and LSS data. The coupling strength needed to appreciably reduce S8S_{8} is around ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)∼1\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}/(H_{0}\rho_{c})\sim 1 (where ρc\rho_{c} is the critical density). While previous work assumed linear theory, Laguë et al. [257] developed a halo-model approach to characterize the behavior of DM with non-zero ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE} on semi-linear scales. This model is an adapted version of HMcode (still assuming dark matter only) and accounts for changes in halo formation resulting from DE-DM interactions using modified fitting functions for the critical and virial overdensities. A combination of CMB lensing from ACT DR6 and Planck, BAO from SDSS/BOSS, and CMB primary anisotropy measurements from Planck constrains the contribution of ΓDMDE/H0​ρc<2.76\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}/H_{0}\rho_{c}<2.76 at the 95% CL using this prescription [257].

Here, we enlarge the dataset to include the new ACT DR6 primary CMB power spectra, and we replace the BAO likelihood with that of DESI.3838 38 We note here that the interacting DE-DM model is the only case in this paper for which we use the extended setting for the ACT DR6 + Planck CMB lensing data. To constrain ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}, we make use of the full CMB lensing likelihood up to L=1250L=1250 [296, 367]. We study two configurations for this model. We first fix the dark energy equation of state to three different values of w∈{−0.999,−0.975,−0.95}w\in\{-0.999,-0.975,-0.95\}, allowing ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE} to vary (the model is thus a two-parameter extension of Λ\LambdaCDM with only one additional degree of freedom). We avoid w=−1w=-1 due to a divergence that arises in Eq. (66) in this case. We then also jointly sample both parameters, but we find that Metropolis-Hastings sampling performs poorly when varying both ww and ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}. This occurs because ww can take a very wide range of values when ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE} goes to 00.3939 39 In this case, due to the computational expense in this model, we stop the chains at a Gelman-Rubin statistic of R−1<0.05R-1<0.05; thus, slight variations in the final bounds are expected. We adopt a flat prior ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)∈[10−8,50]\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}/(H_{0}\rho_{c})\in[10^{-8},50]. We compute theoretical predictions for this scenario using the modified version of class from [257].4040 40 https://github.com/fmccarthy/Class_DMDE

We show the parameter posterior distributions for a subset of the runs in Fig. 38. Given the large degeneracies present in this model when using only CMB data, we focus on results for the data combinations P-ACT-LB and P-ACT-LBS. For fixed values of ww, we find that the limit on ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)\Gamma_{\mathrm{DMDE}}/(H_{0}\rho_{\mathrm{c}}) gets tighter moving away from the w=−1w=-1 boundary: ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)w=−0.999<3.10\Gamma_{\mathrm{DMDE}}/(H_{0}\rho_{\mathrm{c}})_{w=-0.999}<3.10, ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)w=−0.975<1.64\Gamma_{\mathrm{DMDE}}/(H_{0}\rho_{\mathrm{c}})_{w=-0.975}<1.64, and ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)w=−0.95<1.64\Gamma_{\mathrm{DMDE}}/(H_{0}\rho_{\mathrm{c}})_{w=-0.95}<1.64 (all at 95% CL from P-ACT-LB). Similarly, the S8S_{8} limit gets tighter, with the low-end tail of the distribution being more excluded (see Fig. 38). When varying ww and ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)\Gamma_{\mathrm{DMDE}}/(H_{0}\rho_{\mathrm{c}}) simultaneously, we find

ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)<1.9​(95%,P-ACT-LB),\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{DMDE}}/(H_{0}\rho_{\mathrm{c}})<1.9\;(95\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LB}),
S8=0.781−0.02+0.04(68%,P-ACT-LB),\displaystyle S_{8}=0.781^{+0.04}_{-0.02}\quad\quad\quad(68\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LB}), (67)

and when including SNIa data from Pantheon+

ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)<2.1​(95%,P-ACT-LBS),\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{DMDE}}/(H_{0}\rho_{\mathrm{c}})<2.1\;(95\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LBS}),
S8=0.780−0.02+0.04(68%,P-ACT-LBS).\displaystyle S_{8}=0.780^{+0.04}_{-0.02}\quad\quad\quad(68\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LBS}). (68)

We also perform the same analyses with BOSS BAO data used in place of DESI, finding similar constraints on S8S_{8} (with error bars 1010-3030% larger) and somewhat weaker bounds on ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE} (roughly 2020-5050% larger upper limits). We see no preference for this model over Λ\LambdaCDM for any dataset combination considered here, with the best-fit model lying at the ΓDMDE=0\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}=0 edge of the parameter space (note that there are no projection effects in the Bayesian posteriors in the cases where we fix ww to specific values). The inclusion of the ACT DR6 and DESI data tightens the upper limit on ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE} by 33% compared to the bounds from [257] when varying both ww and ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE} using the P-ACT-LB dataset. The improvement in constraining power comes mainly from using the DESI BAO dataset instead of BOSS and the improved bounds on Ωm\Omega_{m} from the primary CMB in ACT DR6. The addition of SNIa data from Pantheon+ does not improve our bounds.

As observed in previous work, the coupling between the DM and DE leads to reduced values of S8S_{8}, significantly broadening the marginalized posterior for this parameter. When −w-w approaches unity, the effects of the coupling are delayed to lower redshifts. This makes CMB lensing, which is sensitive to redshifts around z∼1−2z\sim 1-2, less constraining for this model. For this reason, we find a more extended posterior for ΓDMDE/(H0​ρc)\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}/(H_{0}\rho_{\rm{c}}) when ww is near −1-1, as shown in Fig. 38. In general, we find that this model allows values of S8S_{8} from P-ACT-LB that are consistent with values found in galaxy weak lensing surveys, but we caution that a joint analysis with such datasets would require a full model for the nonlinear matter power spectrum in this scenario.

VII.4 Modified gravity

The growth rate of large-scale structure f⁡(a)≡d​ln⁡D⁡(a)/d​ln⁡af(a)\equiv d\ln D(a)/d\ln a, where D⁡(a)D(a) is the linear growth factor and aa is the scale factor, can be accurately approximated in the matter- or dark energy-dominated eras as

f⁡(a)=Ωmγ​(a),f(a)=\Omega_{m}^{\gamma}(a)\,, (69)

where γ\gamma is the growth index, which takes a canonical value of 0.55 in general relativity (GR) with a flat Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology [170, 444, 282]. This simple model with values of γ\gamma differing from 0.55 is part of a broader class of modified gravity theories, which generically predict modifications to the growth of structure. Various studies have considered and constrained different prescriptions for the growth and geometry [445, 187, 140, 214, 369, 365, 384, 63, 233, 14, 313, 49, 129, 173, 386, 385, 450, 27, 101, 131, e.g.,]. Some studies have found evidence for suppression of the growth of structure, while others have not. One of the most sensitive datasets for such theories is the combination f​σ8​(z)f\sigma_{8}(z) (the product of f⁡(z)f(z) and σ8​(z)\sigma_{8}(z)) which is constrained by various redshift-space distortion (RSD) and peculiar velocity surveys. RSD surveys measure the growth rate of structure via the imprint of peculiar velocities on the quadrupole of redshift-space galaxy clustering measurements [237, 189, 341, 416, e.g.,]. Surveys of the peculiar velocities of individual galaxies can be performed at low-to-moderate redshifts, when an estimate of the absolute distance to each galaxy is available (e.g., from Cepheid, TRGB, or SNIa observations), thus allowing the cosmological contribution to the observed redshift to be isolated from the peculiar-velocity contribution [305, 374, 435, 434, 419, e.g.,]. CMB data also contribute constraining power via lensing effects [94, e.g.,].

A recent analysis by [325] found moderate evidence of a potential deviation from the GR prediction for γ\gamma. They considered measurements of peculiar velocities from [78], [218], [438], and [388], and measurements of RSD from [65], [212], [68], [69], [344], [16], and [328]. Combining these with data from Planck, they found evidence for suppression of the growth of structure at 3.7​σ3.7\sigma significance, with γ=0.639−0.025+0.024\gamma=0.639^{+0.024}_{-0.025}. This suppression both significantly reduced S8S_{8} and eliminated Planck’s (mild) preference for positive spatial curvature.

Here, we study the impact of including the new ACT DR6 spectra on these results, following the approach of [325]. Since Eq. (69) is only valid for sub-horizon perturbations, this approach leaves the unlensed primary CMB perturbations unchanged, but modifies the CMB lensing potential and other late-time observables self-consistently. We use all measurements considered by [325] to form a f​σ8f\sigma_{8} likelihood, consisting of a simple Gaussian likelihood for each survey’s constraint on f​σ8f\sigma_{8}. DESI also recently released f​σ8f\sigma_{8} measurements [134] which we do not include here to facilitate comparison with [325], but we discuss them in §VIII.1. In combination with ACT and other datasets, we use the f​σ8f\sigma_{8} likelihood to constrain the growth index γ\gamma as a single-parameter extension to Λ\LambdaCDM, varied with a uniform prior γ∈[0,2]\gamma\in\left[0,2\right]. To perform the theoretical calculations, we use the modified version of camb released by [325].4141 41 https://github.com/MinhMPA/CAMB_GammaPrime_Growth

With the new DR6 spectra, we find the growth index to be γ=0.560±0.110\gamma=0.560\pm 0.110, with S8=0.872±0.042​(68%,ACT)S_{8}=0.872\pm 0.042~(68\%,\textsf{ACT}). Combining with Planck, these limits tighten significantly, yielding γ=0.688±0.071\gamma=0.688\pm 0.071 and S8=0.812±0.017​(68%,P-ACT)S_{8}=0.812\pm 0.017\;(68\%,\textsf{P-ACT}). Further adding CMB lensing and DESI BAO data, we obtain

γ=0.663±0.052S8=0.799±0.012} (68%, P-ACT-LB).\left.\begin{aligned} \gamma&=&0.663\pm 0.052\\ S_{8}&=&0.799\pm 0.012\;\end{aligned}\quad\right\}\mbox{{\; (68\%, {P-ACT-LB}).}} (70)

This value of γ\gamma lies 2.2​σ2.2\sigma above the GR prediction, but is nevertheless consistent with it (as shown in Fig. 39).

When replacing the DESI BAO data with BOSS BAO data, we obtain γ=0.635±0.053\gamma=0.635\pm 0.053 and S8=0.812±0.013​(68%,P-ACT-LBBOSS)S_{8}=0.812\pm 0.013\;(68\%,\textsf{P-ACT-LB${}_{\textsf{BOSS}}$}), which is consistent with the P-ACT-LB result but moves closer to the GR expectation. Including now the f​σ8f\sigma_{8} measurements, we obtain4242 42 We note that when including f​σ8f\sigma_{8} measurements, for the BOSS likelihood we use a likelihood that combines BAO and RSD data from BOSS DR12 and eBOSS DR16, as described in [149]. When we refer to P-ACT-LBBOSS{}_{\textsf{BOSS}}-fσ8\sigma_{8} or W-ACT-LBBOSS{}_{\textsf{BOSS}}-fσ8\sigma_{8}, this is the BOSS likelihood that is used.

γ=0.630±0.023S8=0.8050±0.0081} (68%, P-ACT-LB-fσ8).\left.\begin{aligned} \gamma&=&0.630\pm 0.023\\ S_{8}&=&0.8050\pm 0.0081\end{aligned}\quad\right\}\mbox{{\; (68\%, {P-ACT-LB}{-f$\sigma_{8}$}).}} (71)

Replacing DESI BAO data with BOSS has minimal impact, giving γ=0.634±0.024\gamma=0.634\pm 0.024 and S8=0.8121±0.0084S_{8}=0.8121\pm 0.0084 (68%, P-ACT-LBBOSS{}_{\textsf{BOSS}}-fσ8\sigma_{8}). The central values of γ\gamma in these constraints deviate from GR at 3.5​σ3.5\sigma. The data driving this result are those from RSD and peculiar velocity surveys, but the central values are consistent with those found in our analyses without these data.

Note that values of γ>0.55\gamma>0.55 can improve concordance between CMB-derived and LSS-derived constraints on S8S_{8}, compared to those in Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}. For example, our P-ACT result in the modified-growth model (S8=0.812±0.017S_{8}=0.812\pm 0.017) is lower than that in Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} (S8=0.830±0.014S_{8}=0.830\pm 0.014, L25). We do not run constraints using non-CMB data on their own, but [325] find that the combination of f​σ8f\sigma_{8}, DES-Y1 3×\times2-point, and pre-DESI BAO data yields S8=0.784−0.016+0.017S_{8}=0.784^{+0.017}_{-0.016} in this model. This agrees with the P-ACT S8S_{8} result at 1.2​σ1.2\sigma, whereas in Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}, the same comparison is discrepant at 3.0​σ3.0\sigma. The moderate tension is reduced in the modified-growth model both by ∼1​σ\sim 1\sigma shifts in the central S8S_{8} values and small increases in the error bars.

The effects of varying γ\gamma on the lensed CMB power spectrum are similar to those from the phenomenological lensing amplitude parameter, AlensA_{\mathrm{lens}} [325], for which Planck has a moderate preference for a value Alens>1A_{\mathrm{lens}}>1 [354]. To assess whether it is the Planck AlensA_{\mathrm{lens}} behavior driving the evidence for a high growth index, we swap in WMAP for Planck data. For the CMB-only combination, we find γ=0.621±0.087\gamma=0.621\pm 0.087 and S8=0.840±0.028​(68%,W-ACT)S_{8}=0.840\pm 0.028\;(68\%,\textsf{W-ACT}). Adding CMB lensing, BOSS BAO, and the f​σ8f\sigma_{8} data yields

γ=0.628±0.022S8=0.8122±0.0091} (68%, W-ACT-LBBOSS-fσ8),\left.\begin{aligned} \gamma&=&0.628\pm 0.022\\ S_{8}&=&0.8122\pm 0.0091\end{aligned}\quad\right\}\mbox{{\; (68\%, {W-ACT-LB${}_{\textsf{BOSS}}$}{-f$\sigma_{8}$}),}} (72)

still finding a 3.5​σ3.5\sigma deviation from the GR value of γ\gamma. This shows that the current evidence for a non-standard growth index is not driven by Planck’s preference for a high CMB lensing amplitude or by DESI BAO data. The precision on this result is driven strongly by the f​σ8f\sigma_{8} data. We discuss in more detail how this f​σ8f\sigma_{8} dataset compares with Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} in §VIII.1. Any preference for this model appears to be largely driven by the f​σ8f\sigma_{8} data (in fact, by just two of these data points) rather than the ACT data or other CMB data, as discussed further in §VIII.1.

VIII Consistency with low-redshift data and impact on cosmological concordance

VIII.1 Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} consistency with low-redshift observations

Given our findings that no model is significantly preferred over Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}, we confirm the consistency of our baseline Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} model (described in L25) with the main low-redshift datasets used here in combination with P-ACT. The agreement between the predictions of the best-fit P-ACT Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} model and direct measurements of the CMB lensing power spectrum, BAO distances, and SNIa distances provides a powerful consistency test of the cosmological model and justifies our joint inclusion of these datasets in Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} and extended model fits.

In Fig. 40, we show predictions for the two main datasets we combine with: ACT DR6+Planck NPIPE CMB lensing and DESI BAO. We find that the P-ACT Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} best-fit model predicts these observations well, and slightly improves the agreement with the DESI data, compared to that seen for the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} model determined by Planck alone. The same figure also shows the combined P-ACT-LB Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} fit to all datasets, including residuals and the probability to exceed (PTE) for CMB lensing and BAO.4343 43 The three models give very similar PTEs for CMB lensing — 34.7%, 35.3%, 35.3% for Planck, P-ACT, and P-ACT-LB, respectively — which round to the same number when reporting only two significant figures. We find here and in L25 that the jointly-derived Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} model is a good fit to all datasets. The residuals and best-fit PTE for Planck and ACT primary CMB power spectra are discussed in L25.

Figure 41 shows the equivalent comparison for the Pantheon+ SNIa compilation. We show the usual Hubble diagram of the distance modulus (corrected apparent magnitude) of all SNIa in the compilation as a function of redshift, and compare it with Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} predictions from the CMB and the joint best-fit model. Differently from [83], we do not normalize the distance modulus using the SH0ES calibration. Instead, we separately obtain and correct for the absolute magnitude calibration from the Planck and P-ACT cosmology. The fit of the joint P-ACT-S dataset marginalizes over this calibration while sampling the cosmological parameters. We find that all Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} solutions are in good agreement with the whole sample, recovering maximum-likelihood values similar to those reported in the Pantheon+ public chains.

Figure 42 shows the data used in the f​σ8f\sigma_{8} likelihood from §VII.4, compared with the theoretical predictions in Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} for f​σ8​(z)f\sigma_{8}(z) from the 68% CL constraints for P-ACT and W-ACT (L25). It appears that the hint of deviation from Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} found in §VII.4 is driven by low-zz points in the f​σ8f\sigma_{8} dataset that have small error bars and lie below the CMB expectation for f​σ8​(z)f\sigma_{8}(z). To assess the difference between the CMB-predicted f​σ8​(z)f\sigma_{8}(z) and the data points from RSD and peculiar velocity surveys, we compute the χ2\chi^{2} between them, finding χ2=28.0\chi^{2}=28.0 with respect to the P-ACT prediction and χ2=37.3\chi^{2}=37.3 with respect to the W-ACT prediction, both for 20 degrees of freedom, indicating some discordance (note, however, that these χ2\chi^{2} values do not propagate the theoretical uncertainty on the CMB predictions). These χ2\chi^{2} values decrease significantly if we omit two of the low-zz peculiar velocity data points that have the lowest f​σ8f\sigma_{8} values. These points are at redshifts z=0.025z=0.025 (from 438, with f​σ8=0.357±0.071f\sigma_{8}=0.357\pm 0.071) and z=0.035z=0.035 (from 388 with f​σ8=0.338±0.027f\sigma_{8}=0.338\pm 0.027). Omitting these points, we find χ2=14.4\chi^{2}=14.4 for the P-ACT prediction and χ2=19.1\chi^{2}=19.1 for W-ACT, both for 18 degrees of freedom, illustrating no tension. Because of the significant χ2\chi^{2} reduction that results from removing the lowest two redshift points, we conclude that deviations from Λ\LambdaCDM when including f​σ8f\sigma_{8} data in §VII.4 are largely driven by those points. In theory, one could redo the analysis omitting those points from the likelihood. However, we do not perform this exercise here since it is not the ACT DR6 data driving these deviations.

Figure 42 also shows recent f​σ8f\sigma_{8} measurements from DESI [134], though these points are not used in our joint likelihood analysis. Assuming a diagonal covariance matrix, we find that the DESI measurements have χ2=4.0\chi^{2}=4.0 with respect to the P-ACT Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} prediction and χ2=4.2\chi^{2}=4.2 with respect to the W-ACT Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} prediction, both for 6 degrees of freedom. Thus, the DESI RSD data are in good agreement with Λ\LambdaCDM, further suggesting that the two outlying f​σ8f\sigma_{8} points at very low-zz are not indicative of new physics.

VIII.2 Cosmological concordance

Many of the models studied in this paper impact the value of the Hubble constant inferred from the primary CMB power spectra, and the precision of the H0H_{0} measurement changes because of parameter degeneracies in these scenarios. In some cases, such as in models with variations in the particle physics content and/or particle interactions, the degeneracies are due to changes in the ingredients of the universe affecting the expansion history at early times. In other cases, for example for the early dark energy model, the physics prior to or at recombination is changed significantly to reduce the sound horizon and this increases the Hubble constant at the expense of additional degrees of freedom in the cosmological model correlating with H0H_{0}. While no robust detection of any of these extended models has been made in previous CMB or LSS data, some of these models have previously had non-negligible success in shifting the CMB-derived H0H_{0} value toward the local distance ladder estimate from SH0ES. In this work, we have shown that this is generally no longer the case when including the new ACT data. ACT DR6 contributes to limiting the allowed region of parameter space to 66.1<H0<71.066.1<H_{0}<71.0 km/s/Mpc within all of the models studied here. This range is calculated as the minimum and maximum value at 68% CL of all the P-ACT-LB and P-ACT-LBS results (whichever yields higher precision) from all models explored in this work; the neutrino self-interaction result from §VI.1.2 sets the lower end of the allowed range and the early dark energy result from §V.1 sets the upper end. This range of values is in agreement with the CCHP measurement [167], but lies below the latest SH0ES measurement [79].

These results are summarized in Fig. 43. Figure 44 provides more details on the full suite of H0H_{0} constraints for the three classes of models that have a non-negligible impact on H0H_{0}. Figure 45 breaks this result further down into the specific behavior of H0H_{0} versus key model parameters in many extended models of interest, and shows that both the CMB-only dataset, P-ACT, and its combination with CMB lensing and BAO, P-ACT-LB, are inconsistent with the SH0ES estimate. Because of correlations with the inferred value of the total matter density Ωm\Omega_{m},4444 44 Note that the primary CMB most directly constrains a degenerate combination of Ωm\Omega_{m} and H0H_{0}, roughly Ωm​h3\Omega_{m}h^{3}, with the exact value of the exponent depending on the range of angular scales measured, due to the different physical effects at play [342, 235, e.g.,]. BAO data play an important role in determining the central value of H0H_{0} in many extended models. Notably, as shown in many of the analyses in §V–§VII, using BOSS BAO instead of DESI data reduces the central value of H0H_{0} by 1–1.5 km/s/Mpc — hence moving constraints in the opposite direction of SH0ES — while only slightly increasing the error bars. Upcoming DESI data will be instrumental in further clarifying this situation.

From a more model-independent perspective, the consistency of the inferred physical matter density Ωm​h2\Omega_{m}h^{2} from Planck and ACT (as well as their combination; L25) within Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} provides a strong indication that the Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} model accurately describes physics just prior to recombination. As noted in [249], the shape of the radiation-driving envelope in the CMB power spectra is directly tied to the physics operating around matter-radiation equality. If new physics were present at this epoch, a generic expectation is that Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}-based inferences of Ωm​h2\Omega_{m}h^{2} should exhibit deviations when inferred on different angular scale ranges, due to different scales probing H⁡(z)H(z) at different times via radiation driving. We see no such evidence of such deviations in Ωm​h2\Omega_{m}h^{2} (L25), thus providing a strong validation of the physics of Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} in this important redshift range.

We also find that models that alter the growth of structure are not preferred by our data. In particular, we do not find evidence in any extended model for a significant shift in the CMB-inferred S8S_{8} value toward lower late-universe estimates, for example from cosmic shear surveys, as summarized in Fig. 46. Our results generally lie on the upper end of the limits from DES+KiDS [121], although it is important to note that the S8S_{8} value in Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} is already consistent between P-ACT-LB and this result.4545 45 The more recent KiDS Legacy measurement, S8=0.815−0.021+0.016S_{8}=0.815^{+0.016}_{-0.021}, shifts to even higher values and is almost perfectly centered on the P-ACT-LB result. Also in this case the matter density inferred via DESI BAO will contribute to the location of the maximum-likelihood point. For all models tested, using BOSS instead of DESI BAO data yields qualitatively similar conclusions. In addition, it is important to note that the inference of S8S_{8} itself from galaxy weak lensing or other late-time data will generally change in the presence of the new physics shown in these models (e.g., non-GR values of γ\gamma or non-zero ΓDMDE\Gamma_{\rm DMDE}), and thus one should take the comparison shown here with a grain of salt. For a high-precision comparison, constraints from late-time data should be self-consistently derived in these extended models, which we leave to future, dedicated analyses.

IX Summary

In this paper, we have used a state-of-the-art CMB primary anisotropy dataset built from new ACT DR6 power spectra combined with large-scale data from the Planck satellite to set constraints on a large suite of extended cosmological models, both testing foundational assumptions made in the standard Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} model and constraining more complex scenarios. We show that the new ACT DR6 data have reached a level of precision competitive with that of Planck for the primary CMB contribution to the constraints, and because of the complementarity of the two datasets — particularly at ℓ>2000\ell>2000 in TT and on essentially all scales measured by ACT in TE and EE — their joint analysis yields significant gains over the sensitivity of Planck alone. We further include ACT and Planck CMB lensing data, BAO data from DESI and SNIa from Pantheon+ to obtain the tightest limits to date on many fundamental physics parameters and cosmological models. To validate the results, we also explore combinations replacing Planck with WMAP large-scale CMB data, and DESI with BAO data from BOSS.

Key takeaways from this work include:

  • •

    We test predictions for the early-universe inflationary epoch, verifying the near-scale-invariance and adiabaticity of the primordial scalar perturbations, and restricting the parameter space for inflation models;

  • •

    We tightly bound the presence of early dark energy, or primordial magnetic fields that would impact the pre-recombination period, as well as variations in fundamental constants or in the monopole temperature of the CMB or the standard recombination history;

  • •

    We measure the properties of neutrinos and find no evidence for new light, relativistic species that are free-streaming, no evidence for non-zero neutrino masses, and no evidence for neutrino self-interactions. We also set limits on primordial helium and deuterium abundances that are consistent with standard BBN predictions and with astrophysical measurements;

  • •

    Dark matter is consistent with the standard collisionless CDM assumption, with no evidence for annihilation or interactions with baryons. We also limit the contribution to DM from ultralight axion-like particles to be no more than 5% at axion masses of 10−2610^{-26} eV;

  • •

    We find no evidence for interactions in the dark sector, either within a single dark radiation component, between dark radiation and dark matter components, or between dark matter and dark energy;

  • •

    Dark energy and late-time gravity generally behave as expected in the standard model (w=−1w=-1 and γ=0.55\gamma=0.55), although we find a moderate hint for time-evolving dark energy with P-ACT-LBS, consistent with (and driven by the BAO and SNIa data from) [137]. Upcoming BAO and SNIa data are expected to clarify the robustness of this hint.

Assessing the preference for each extended model over Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} via the marginalized posterior for the extended-model parameter (in the case of 1D extensions) or via comparison of the MAP model to that in Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} (in the case of multi-parameter extensions), we find that no extended model is preferred over Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM}. This conclusion includes a wide range of extended models constructed with the aim of increasing the value of the Hubble constant or decreasing the amplitude of density fluctuations inferred from the primary CMB. With these results providing stringent tests in new observational regimes, the footing of the standard model of cosmology is further solidified.

This work paves the way for further, higher-precision tests of the cosmological model in the coming decade with even more sensitive CMB polarization data, including that expected from the Simons Observatory [405, 6], CMB-S4 [112, 1], LiteBIRD [283], and other experiments. The noise levels of these surveys will push nearly an order of magnitude below those of ACT DR6 over the next 10-15 years, enabling precise searches for new physics, including not only the models studied in this work, but also new scenarios yet to be constructed.

Shortly after the appearance of this paper, new BAO measurements from three years of DESI observations and corresponding cosmological interpretation were presented in [138, 139]. In Appendix G, we present updated Λ​CDM\Lambda\rm{CDM} consistency and evolving dark energy constraints from this new dataset, finding results similar to those presented in the main text with DESI Year-1 observations and consistent with those reported in [174]. We also present updated constraints on a subset of the extended models studied earlier in the paper. In addition, we show that relaxing the constraint on the optical depth leads to slightly reduced evidence for w0/waw_{0}/w_{a} and more relaxed bounds on the neutrino mass.
